drills.title: vs Bodda_74 (684) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: Look at your queen on f6 — it's not just attacking, it's the only thing holding your bishop on d4 together, sitting on the f6-e5-d4 diagonal. Qe6 steps off that diagonal, and White's queen on g4 grabs it: Qxe6, Rxe6, and now nothing guards d4, so Rxd4 just wins the bishop for free, turning your small edge into you being down a full piece. The fix is c5 — it leaves the queen on f6 exactly where it is, so d4 stays covered, while hitting White's b4 pawn and opening the a-file for your rook. Before you move a piece, ask what job it was quietly doing.

drills.coachNote: Your knight on g4 is hanging for free, and worse, the g-file is wide open all the way to your own king since your g7 pawn is long gone — so Qxg4 comes with check. Bb5 ignores this entirely: after Qxg4+ Kf8, White's queen swings to h5 with real threats, and you've lost a knight for nothing, wiping out the edge you had. h5 was the move that faces the problem head-on — you let White take on g4 with the h-pawn, recapture hxg4, and now your h-file is open for your rook while f5 comes next hitting the bishop on e4. The knight becomes a paid-for battering ram instead of a free gift.

drills.title: vs Racheeeedgr (827) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: You were up close to three pawns here, and g6 does nothing to cash that in — it doesn't activate your queen, doesn't help your king, it just creates a fresh hole on f6 and h6. White punishes the passivity immediately with Qc4+, and after Kh7, g4 lets White start consolidating and generating counterplay, and your winning edge evaporates. Qb5 was the move that actually works — it keeps your queen active and central, ready to answer Kg2 with Kf8 and trade ideas with Qd7 while your own king marches up. In queen endings, every move should either activate your king or restrict the enemy queen; g6 did neither.

drills.coachNote: You were winning, but jumping the knight to e4 skips checking what White's queen on c5 can do first — Qf5+ comes with check, forcing Kh8, and only then does White scoop the knight with Qxe4, since nothing was covering that square. That's a full piece gone from a position where you were simply better. Qe8 was the calm move instead — it brings the queen off the back rank into play and meets Qc2+ with Kh8, keeping the knight home and the edge intact. Before hopping a piece into the center, run through every queen check first — checks change the board before your move even lands.

drills.coachNote: Your b4 pawn was already undefended, nothing was watching it, so it was going regardless of what you played. Kf3 just wastes the move while your knight on g5 sits offside, and after Rxb4 you're forced to walk the king back with Ke2, burning two tempi while Black's rook gets fully active on a4 and the e-pawn rolls forward. Nf3 was the better use of that tempo — it starts rerouting the knight toward d4, a monster central square, so even though b4 still falls eventually, you've improved your worst piece and grabbed kingside play with f4-g5 first. When a pawn's lost no matter what, spend the move improving your worst piece, not shuffling the king.

drills.coachNote: Your rook on c2 was the only thing defending c3, and Rd2 pulls it off the c-file — the instant you do that, Black's rook on c4 just takes with Rxc3, and your advantage shrinks fast. drills.coachNote: Your king on g6 is way out in the open, and White has a bishop on c4, a knight on g5, and a queen on h4 all aimed at it, covering the escape squares around it. Rh8 does nothing about that, and Bxf7 is instant mate — the bishop takes f7 with check, and there's nowhere to run because g5, h6, and f5/f6 are all covered by White's pieces. Nh5 was the move that faced the danger — it forces the issue immediately, and after Qxg4 Qxg5 Qxg5+ Kxg5 the queens and dangerous attackers come off the board entirely, letting your material edge matter in a safe position instead of getting you mated. When your king is this exposed, every move has to answer for the king first.

Nc6 was the better use of that move — it develops a piece still sitting at home and adds pressure on the center, and even if White still finds Qg3 and later Bxh6, you've got Nh5 hitting the queen with tempo to fight back. A move that attacks a piece only helps if the square it retreats to is actually worse for your opponent — here it wasn't.

drills.coachNote: Your king on e2 has no escape squares — d1, d2 and c2 are all occupied by your own pieces. Black's queen on h2 and that pawn on g3 are both aiming at f2, so the second you play Rh1 to chase the queen sideways, she just plays Qxf2# — mate, because f2 isn't guarded and the king can't run anywhere. Rxg3 was the move: it removes the pawn fueling the mating idea instead of ignoring it, and the line continues Bd6, Nf1, Qh5+ — messy, but you're alive. drills.coachNote: Black's queen on g2 is the danger here — the question is how you actually kick her out. Rg1 only pressures her along the g-file, so she simply slides to h3, grabbing that pawn and staying active — that's the Qxh3, Nbd2, Ne7, Qa4+ line where your edge shrinks fast. Rh2 does the job better: attacking along the second rank instead, it takes away h3 as an escape, forcing Qxh2, Nxh2 and a straight queen trade. With queens off you're just up material and development — Bd7, c4, O-O-O is a comfortable game. When you attack a queen, check every square she can run to, not just the ones your piece covers.

Instead g4 gave black a free tempo — Rd1+ chased your king to g2, then Rd5 got the rook active, and only after that did you finally play Rxc3 anyway, four moves late. Rxf4 abandoned that rook — Qxe8+ snapped it off with check, and after Kh7, Qe6 left White completely consolidated. Taking with the wrong piece cost about six pawns.

drills.coachNote: Your rook on e8 sat on the exact same diagonal as White's queen on h5 - h5-g6-f7-e8 - the whole time, so grabbing the knight on f4 with your rook left e8 completely undefended. White answers Qxe8+ immediately, and you've traded a whole rook for a knight, a swing of six pawns that turned a level game into a loss. Qxf4 captures that same knight while keeping your rook safely tucked on e8 out of the queen's line, leading to a normal fight after Qe2 e3 fxe3 Rxe3. Before any capture, glance at what you're leaving behind on the back rank, not just what you're picking up.

drills.explanation: a6 strikes at White's overextended queenside: after bxa6 Rxa6 your rook enters the game down the a-file, and b5 is met calmly by Ra8. Castling let White play Qe2, hitting your knight on c4 — a piece with no defenders — and you had to scramble with c6 and b5 just to hold it, leaving White a wedge pawn on c6.
drills.title: vs prusten63 (873) — Italian Game
drills.coachNote: White's pawn on b5 was hanging out there ripe for ...a6 right now - bxa6 Rxa6 and your rook swings to a6, active and pressing, while your structure stays sound. Instead castling let White play Qe2 and then push c6, cracking open the queenside and planting a strong, cramping pawn near your own camp that's a long-term headache rather than a one-move fix. Castling isn't wrong in general, but the position had a ticking clock here - the moment for ...a6 was right then, before White got to reinforce b5 and start that c6 break himself. Look for the live pawn lever before defaulting to routine development.

drills.explanation: You were a full piece up and just needed to consolidate. c5 gains space, and the knight calmly reroutes to c6 next with b6 and normal development to follow. Ng4 put the knight on a square covered by White's queen all the way back on d1 — Qxg4 took it for nothing, handing the extra piece straight back.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Your knight jumped from e5 to g4 without noticing White's queen on d1 covers that square clean, along the d1-e2-f3-g4 diagonal, and nothing of yours was watching it. Qxg4 just wins the knight for free, no combination needed, and that single oversight is the whole 4.5 pawn swing, from a roughly even game to a piece down. c5 was simply the right idea instead - expanding on the queenside where your knight on c4 already has support, keeping every piece safe while you build. Before you move a piece to an empty-looking square, trace every line and diagonal a queen or bishop already has open toward it - g4 was sitting right on one.

drills.explanation: Bxa2 trades off White's light-squared bishop on your terms: after Rxa2 you swing rooks to the e-file with Rae8 and Re6, sitting solidly behind the e5 pawn. Rad8 left the bishops eyeballing each other one move too long — Bh6 came with threats at your king, and after g6, Bxe6 fxe6 left you with doubled, weak e-pawns.
drills.opening: Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.title: vs Feri206 (798) — Caro Kann Defense Two Knights Attack
drills.coachNote: Your bishop on e6 was staring straight down the a2-g8 diagonal at White's own bishop on a2 with nothing in between, so Bxa2 Rxa2 was a clean, even trade that opens the e-file for your rook to get active. Instead Rad8 let White play Bh6, threatening your king's cover, and you're forced into ...g6 to survive it - after which Bxe6 fxe6 trades that same bishop off anyway, except now your e-pawns are doubled and your king is more exposed. You'd already given back a piece earlier in this game, so every extra weakening here costs more, not less. When a favorable trade is sitting there for free, take it before your opponent forces the same trade on worse terms.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 wins a full rook: the knight captures its counterpart and forks the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so after Qd6 saves the queen, Nxd8 collects the rook and Qxg5 even adds a pawn. a4 instead gave Black time for Nxe5, trading off your monster knight, and after Qxe5 his other knight landed on e4 with real counterplay.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Look at your knight on c5 - it had Nxc6 available, forking Black's queen on e7 and rook on d8 at once, since a knight landing on c6 hits both squares simultaneously. That wins material outright: Qd6, Nxd8, Qxd8, and you're up the exchange with your other knight still dominating e5. Instead a4 let the moment slip, and Black seized the initiative with Nxe5, trading down and following with Ne4, hitting your pawns on c3 and f2 and clawing back over four pawns of your advantage. Before reaching for a slower move like a4, scan your active knights first for forcing forks - c5 and e5 both deserved a second look before a pawn push.

drills.explanation: Nxc6 is a fork: from c6 the knight hits both the queen on e7 and the rook on d8, so bxc6 is forced — wrecking the pawn cover in front of the king on c8. Then Qd3 turns on the knight on e4, and after Nxc5 bxc5 you're clearly on top. b5 abandoned the b4 pawn's guard of your c5 knight, and Nxe5 won material — no recapture worked.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs TheArtifier (833) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Before playing b5, look at your knight on e5 — it's actually hanging. Your queen on e3 is supposed to guard it down the e-file, but Black's own knight on e4 sits right in that line and blocks the defense completely. b5 ignores this and just nudges the c6 knight, so Black answers Nxe5, winning a full piece — that's your 4.5-pawn swing, from +1.2 to lost. Nxc6 first was the fix: trade off the attacker before pushing pawns. After Nxc6 bxc6 Qd3, material stays level and you're fine. Always check what's actually defending a piece, not just that it looks defended.

drills.explanation: Rxf7 forces mate in three: your queen on d5 X-rays g8 so f7 can't really be held, and after Rg7+ Kh8, Rg8 is checkmate — the bishop on f6 seals g7 while the queen on d5 guards g8, so the rook can't be taken. Qg5 instead let Black play Rxf2 and keep the counterplay alive.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: Black's king on g8 is boxed in by its own pawns on f7, g6 and h7, with your bishop on f6 and rooks doubled on the e-file. Rxf7! rips the last shield away — Rxf7 Re2 Rg7+ Kh8 Rg8# is forced mate. Instead you played Qg5, and even with a position this crushing, you let Black grab Rxf2 with the rook on c2 — dangerous, since your own king only has the f2 pawn for cover, g2 and h2 are open behind it. Suddenly Qe5, Rf3, Rf1 come crawling at you and +20 shrinks to barely +2. When mate is on the board, play the forcing capture, not the fancy queen move.

drills.explanation: Qxc8 wins the rook on c8 outright — Black never dares recapture, since your bishop on f6 and rook on e7 strangle his king; he tries Qb5, and after Re8 he must throw his queen away with Qf1+ Rxf1. Qd5 let a won game slip: Qxa3, and after Qxd4, Qxh3 stripped your king — nearly fifteen pawns of advantage gone.
drills.title: vs yassine3453 (860) — Englund Gambit
drills.coachNote: The rook on c8 is completely undefended — nothing Black has reaches it. Qxc8! just wins it outright, your queen on c4 has a clear run up the c-file. Instead Qd5 repositions for no real reason, and Black's queen comes alive: Qxa3 grabs a pawn right by your own king, then Qxd4 Qxh3 and suddenly Black's queen is tearing through your kingside pawns, costing you a move (R7e3) just to hold on — nearly 15 pawns of advantage gone. With Qxc8 Qb5 Re8 Qf1+ Rxf1, you're simply up a full rook instead. When you're already crushing, grab the free piece before chasing anything fancier.

drills.explanation: The g5 pawn was attacking your bishop on f4, and Nxg5 meets that head-on — the knight is covered by that same bishop, and after fxg5 Bxg5 Black's kingside pawns are stripped while his pieces retreat to passive squares like Nf6 and Nb8 as Qf3 builds pressure. Bf5+ dropped a whole piece instead: e6 blocked the check and hit the bishop, and after Bc2, gxf4 won your dark-squared bishop.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Bf5+ feels natural, but Black just plays e6, blocking the check while attacking your bishop, so you're forced to retreat it to the passive c2 square. Worse, that whole detour ignores your other bishop on f4, which nothing defends — Black grabs it with gxf4 and you're down a full piece for nothing. The real story here is Black's king stuck on d7; e4! is what actually exploits that, ripping the center open. After e4 gxf4 exd5 Na7 Qa4+, you're the one delivering checks with real threats, not just trading pieces off. Only play a check when you've worked out what happens after it's answered — here the answer cost you a whole piece.

drills.explanation: Nxg5 was the shot: after fxg5 Bxg5 you get two pawns for the knight and Black's king on d7 is stranded, with Qf3 coming to hit the loose d5 pawn (the simple e4 was strong too). Bf5+ backfired — e6 blocked with tempo, the bishop crawled back to c2, and gxf4 scooped up your dark-squared bishop, which the g5 pawn had been eyeing all along.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs jatin221272 (817) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Same pattern as a few moves back — Bf5+ walks into e6, forcing the bishop to the dead square c2, while your other bishop on f4 just hangs to gxf4. That's a piece lost for a check that achieved nothing. This time the sharpest idea was Nxg5!, sacrificing the knight to blast open the kingside in front of Black's king, still stuck on d7 and uncastled: after Nxg5 fxg5 Bxg5, you're already winning material back and your bishop and queen bear down on that king. Following with Nf6 Qf3 keeps the pressure rolling. The lesson worth carrying forward: when the enemy king is stuck in the center, look for lines that rip it open, not a hollow check.

drills.explanation: Your knight on e4 was attacked by the d3 pawn, and Nd6 is the safe retreat — White wins the e5 pawn with Rxe5+, but Be7 blocks, Bg6 follows, and you're only down a pawn with pieces coming out. Ng5 ran the knight straight onto the c1-bishop's diagonal: Bxg5 won it outright, and White grabbed e5 with the knight as well.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Your knight jumps to g5 to hit the f3 knight, but g5 itself is wide open — White's bishop on c1 has a clear diagonal all the way to h6, and Bxg5 just wins your knight for nothing. Then f6 Nxe5 and White scoops the e5 pawn too, so one move costs you a piece and a pawn. The safer path was Nd6, pulling the attacked knight back to safety; White still nets the e5 pawn with check (Rxe5+ Be7), but that's just a pawn, not a piece, and you finish developing with Qe2 Bg6 Bf4. Before sending a piece to attack something, always check whether the square it's landing on is itself covered.

drills.explanation: Your knight on g5 was attacked by the bishop on c1, defended only by your queen along the d8–g5 diagonal — and Be7 blocked that exact diagonal. Bxg5 won the knight, and after Be6, Bxe7 Qxe7 left White a clean piece up. Ne6 just steps to safety; after Qf3 Qf6 Nxc6 Bxd3 the position stays a fair fight.
drills.title: vs Stwilso1 (836) — Ruy Lopez Opening Berlin Defense
drills.coachNote: Same hole you just fell into — your knight is still on g5, still hanging to that bishop on c1 down the open c1-h6 diagonal. Be7 develops a piece but does nothing about the actual threat, so White plays Bxg5, and after Be6 Bxe7 Qxe7 you've lost the knight outright while only trading bishops back. The fix was Ne6 — move the piece that's actually under attack, not a different one. After Ne6 Qf3 Qf6 you're still fully in the game, even picking up chances like Bxd3 later. Rule to carry forward: when one of your pieces is hanging, dealing with that always comes before any developing move.

drills.explanation: Bc7 hits the queen on d8 and grabs a square deep in Black's camp: after Qd7, b6 locks the bishop on c7 permanently, cramping the whole queenside while Ra4 swings the rook toward the action. Your e4 gave Black a free move for Bd7, developing with a hit on the b5 pawn — the same Bc7 idea then came a tempo late, and the queen slipped away to c8.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: You're winning here, but your bishop on f4 has a shot at c7 — Bc7 hits the queen on d8 directly, forcing it to move on your terms. Instead e4 looks reasonable but hands Black a free tempo: Bd7 develops and Qc8 tucks the queen away safely before you ever get around to playing Bc7 yourself, so by the time you do, Black's already organized and your initiative has cooled by over two pawns. With Bc7 first, Qd7 is forced, then b6 cramps Black's queenside and Ra4 lifts your rook into the attack. When you spot a move that hits something with tempo, play that before a slower positional push.

drills.explanation: Qc5 does three jobs: it confronts the queen on b6, attacks the knight on e7, and keeps the b5 pawn defended. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7, and Bxe7 Rxe7 leaves you in full control of the dark squares. Qc3 left b5 with no defender at all — Bd7 came immediately, and after your too-late Qc5, Bxb5 took the pawn for free.
drills.title: vs slammerman001 (850) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Look at what's loose in his camp: the knight on e7 and the queen on b6 are both reachable in one shot. Qc5 is that shot — your queen jumps to c5 and hits both of them at once along the diagonal, a double attack he can't parry in one move. After Qd8, Bd6 piles onto e7 again and Bxe7 just wins the piece. Qc3 ignores both targets and does nothing for your b5 pawn either, so Bd7 swings onto the long diagonal and picks it off for free while your queen sits idle on c3. Before you pick a queen square, scan what it attacks, not just what it defends.

drills.explanation: Nf5+ is a fork: it checks the king on g3 and attacks the rook on g7 at the same time. After Kf4 you play Nxg7, winning the rook and flipping the game — roughly twelve pawns of swing. Nb7 instead walked into Rc7+, and after Kd8 the rook simply captured the knight on b7.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: You were completely winning here, a piece up with his king boxed in on g3, and the board was screaming Nf5+ — a fork with check. He has to move the king, say Kf4, and then Nxg7 just cleans up his rook for free. Instead Nb7 drops your knight on a square nothing defends, and Rc7+ punishes it instantly: your king's forced to d8, and Rxb7 takes the knight you walked into it — a totally winning endgame flips into a lost one. When you're up material like this, every knight move deserves a two-second check: is this square actually covered by his rook or king right now?

drills.explanation: Bxg3+ wins a pawn with check, and after the forced Kxg3, Rxd1 scoops the rook — d1 had no defender at all, so you net rook and pawn for the bishop. Rd7 put your rook on a square nothing defends (the knight on c6 doesn't cover d7): Rxd7 took it for free, and after Bd6, bxc6 grabbed your knight as well.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.title: vs OdisseoAP (826) — Queens Pawn Opening Zukertort Chigorin Variation
drills.coachNote: Notice your bishop on f4 has a free hit on g3 — Bxg3+ is check on his king on h2, so he's forced into Kxg3, which pulls him away from defending the rook on d1. Then Rxd1 just wins that rook clean, since nothing else guards it, on top of the knight you're already up. Instead Rd7 slides your rook straight down the same file his rook already sits on, onto a square nothing of yours defends — Rxd7 takes it for free, and a completely winning position collapses into you being down the exchange. Before landing a rook on an open file, check whether his rook is staring right back at that square.

drills.explanation: Qxb7+ forces checkmate: the queen grabs b7 and checks the king on e7 along the wide-open seventh rank, Black must block with Qc7, and Qxc7 is mate — your knight on f6 covers the escape squares e8 and d7, and the e5 pawn guards the knight. exd4 was a pawn grab with mate on the board; after Bg7 Black started breathing again.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: His king is stuck on e7 in the middle of the board, and your queen on f3 has a totally clear diagonal all the way to b7, with check, because rank 7 is wide open behind it. Qxb7+ forces Qc7 as the only block, and Qxc7# is just mate — his king has nowhere to run with your knight on f6 covering the exits. Instead exd4 just grabs a pawn and lets him play Bg7, hitting your knight on f6 and giving him room to untangle — you're still winning, but you traded a forced mate for a long grind. When a king is this exposed, scan the diagonals and open files pointing at it before reaching for a quiet recapture.

drills.explanation: Rd7+ is a deflection: the queen on c7 has to capture, and Nxd7 then forks the rook on b8 and the bishop on f8 — you've won queen for rook, with Rd1 coming to support the knight. Nd7 tried the fork without the preparation: Bg7 simply stepped the bishop out, nothing was won, and Rd6 got met by Rbc8. The open d-file was the key — use it with check first.
drills.opening: Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.title: vs pisitto999 (814) — Queens Pawn Opening Accelerated London System
drills.coachNote: Your rook on d1 has a wide-open file staring straight at his king on e7 — Rd7+ is check, and it's really a sacrifice: he has to answer with Qxd7 since that's the only way to deal with the check, and then Nxd7 — your knight on f6 just scoops up his queen. You come out a queen for a rook, completely crushing. Instead Nd7 forks his rook on b8 and bishop on f8, which looks tempting, but he simply saves them one at a time with Bg7 then Rbc8, leaving you with a nice edge instead of winning his queen outright. When you spot a fork, always check first whether a check wins even more.

drills.explanation: Your queen on a4 was attacked by the knight on c5 and had to reach safety first — Qa3 does it. The Qh4 attacking idea was right but needed f6 first: after f6 gxf6, Black's own pawn on f6 blocks the e7–h4 diagonal, and only then is Qh4 strong. Played immediately, Qh4 landed right on the e7-queen's diagonal — Qxh4 won your queen on the spot.
drills.title: vs Iamastalemate (860) — Indian Game
drills.coachNote: Before you slide a queen anywhere, check what diagonal it lands on — his queen on e7 has a completely clear line all the way to h4, e7-f6-g5-h4, nothing in between and nothing of yours guarding that square. Qh4 walks right onto it, so Qxh4 just wins your queen outright, turning an already-uncomfortable position into a lost one. Qa3 was the move: it keeps your queen off that diagonal and still active, and the game stays a normal fight — Re8, c4, d4, worse for you but very much alive. The habit to build: before landing a piece on a square, trace every line his pieces control through it first.
